title: Why start-up counts can miss the source of productivity growth
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: The number of firms being founded is a poor guide to the supply of innovation in the Danish evidence assembled by Akcigit, Alp, Pearce and Prato. The firms that recruit technical workers start larger and grow much faster over their first decade. The authors identify a connection between those findings and access to education. Technical education supplies the people who can develop ideas, but also some of the future owners who will employ them. In their model, a policy that relaxes education finance constraints therefore acts on both sides of the market for research workers. The distinction matters when using entrepreneurship data to judge an economy's long-run capacity to grow.

The definition does considerable work. A founder is the registered primary founder of a business with at least one employee. The authors classify a founder as transformative if the business employs at least one person in a high-patenting occupation. That is an observable hiring decision that can precede innovation. It does not require an actual patent or demonstrated productivity gain. The linked Danish records also identify education, family backgrounds and an ability measure from a military test typically taken early in adulthood. The exercise consequently describes a selected population of founders and a particular observable dimension of technical activity. It tells us little directly about innovative own-account businesses or firms commissioning their technical work externally (section on entrepreneurs).

The first two charts illustrate how the aggregate can give the opposite impression to the subgroup. Moving up the test-score distribution, the fraction of people in each decile who work in R&D rises, while the fraction who found businesses falls. Splitting founders according to technical hiring reverses the relationship for the transformative group. The overall decline reflects the numerically larger group that does not make such a hire. The denominator is the population in a test-score decile. These are not shares of all business owners divided into deciles. The relationships persist after controlling for age, parental background and education. Education is associated with a similar pattern, while having an entrepreneurial parent is the strongest predictor of becoming a founder of any kind.

The operating outcomes make these distinctions economically material. Firms that hire technical talent start with about twice the employment of the other group and record average annual employment growth of 16% against 8%. In the employment chart each group starts at an index value of one, so its subsequent separation captures growth even after setting aside the initial difference in size. By year ten, revenues for the two groups are about seven and two and a half times their respective initial levels. The difference is less pronounced in survival. First-year exit rates are 12% for the transformative firms and 16% for the others, converging to roughly 8–9% by year eight. Technical hiring therefore identifies a group with substantially different expansion paths even though the groups' annual probabilities of exit become similar. These are group comparisons, with industry composition differing across founders, rather than an estimate of the return from adding a research employee at any given firm.

To examine growth policy the authors simulate individual career choices, access to education and the subsequent choice to become a founder. The model matches several observed patterns before being used for a counterfactual in which education finance constraints disappear. In that exercise the workforce share of technical workers rises by 15%, the share of transformative entrepreneurs by 7%, and the pace of economic growth by 11%. These are relative changes in model outcomes, not percentage-point changes in Danish growth or measured effects of a policy already enacted. High-ability people from lower-income families account for much of the adjustment. An exercise that captures only the extra supply of research workers delivers about 60% of the total growth effect. The remaining 40% comes from the additional demand for talent as the pool of innovative founders expands (macroeconomic model section).

For small initial budgets the model assigns subsidies for technical education roughly four times the initial return of subsidies for research or for business formation. The authors also see scope for combining policies as supply and demand adjust. The relevant investment inference is about the timing and quality of productive capacity. A sharp rise in registrations could leave the innovative sector little changed; an expansion in education might work through both payrolls and future founding decisions over a much longer horizon. The study does not estimate how the resulting gains are split between wages, private profits and consumers, so a larger economy-wide return cannot by itself establish a return to holders of a particular asset.

questions.question: How early does the technical-hiring measure identify a genuinely different productivity trajectory?
questions.detail: The source shows divergent employment and revenue, alongside different industry choices. Investors need to distinguish prescient hiring from success that already gave firms the ability to recruit. Use the authors' cited working paper and matched firm accounts to compare productivity and revenues before and after a first technical hire within industries, accounting for outsourcing, initial size and later exits.

questions.question: How much of the education-policy result depends on new firms creating demand for research workers?
questions.detail: Two fifths of the growth gain in the simulation comes from additional entrepreneurial demand. That contribution is important to the pay-off from education spending if technical labour can otherwise accumulate in existing employers. Check the working paper's calibration and sensitivity exercises, then look for administrative evidence on whether marginal recipients of financing become founders, enter established firms or leave the local labour market.

questions.question: Who captures the gains, and over what horizon?
questions.detail: The paper projects aggregate growth and documents faster growth in firm revenues. It does not trace wages, operating margins or investor dilution along those paths. A portfolio thesis requires a bridge from productivity to investable cash flows. Compare payroll, financing and operating-profit histories for successive firm cohorts, including failed firms, before attributing the model's long-run social return to listed firms or venture investors.
